title: From Amritsar to Harvard Yard: Vikas Khanna Named Person of the Year by the University's South Asian Association
excerpt: The Michelin-starred chef, novelist, and filmmaker called the honour 'a promise to continue honouring our culture through every dish, every detail.'
body:
When Vikas Khanna stepped onto the stage at Harvard University this week to accept the South Asian Association's Person of the Year award, the moment distilled a journey that has taken him from the narrow bylanes of Amritsar to the uppermost echelons of global cuisine — and cemented his role as perhaps the most visible cultural ambassador Indian food has ever produced.

## The Honour

The Harvard South Asian Association, one of the university's most active cultural organisations, bestowed the Person of the Year title on Khanna in recognition of what it called his "enormous commitment to showcasing India's rich culinary legacy on the international scene." The honour is both a personal milestone and a broader acknowledgement: it signals that Indian cuisine has penetrated not just America's restaurant scene and grocery aisles but its most prestigious academic institutions.

"What a milestone for Indian cuisine," Khanna said upon accepting the award. "To be named Person of the Year by Harvard University's SAA is beyond words. This recognition is not just an award — it's a promise. A commitment to continue honouring our culture through every dish, every detail."

## The Amritsar-to-New-York Arc

Khanna's story is by now well known in the diaspora but bears recounting. Born and raised amid the bustling street food culture of Amritsar, he arrived in the United States with limited resources and a conviction that Indian food could transcend the buffet-house stereotype. He worked his way through New York kitchens, eventually earning a Michelin star — an accomplishment that put him alongside a vanishingly small number of Indian chefs in the West to achieve that distinction.

But Khanna has always been more than a chef. His 2015 documentary *The Last Color*, set against the taboo-breaking Holi celebrations of widows in Vrindavan, was India's official submission for the Academy Awards. He has authored more than 30 books, including *Utsav*, a landmark compendium of India's culinary heritage. He serves as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef India, where his influence reaches millions of home cooks. And Kinara, his fine-dining restaurant in Dubai, is among the most lauded Indian establishments in the Gulf.

## Culinary Diplomacy in Practice

The Harvard honour arrives at a time when Indian food's stature in America is climbing rapidly. Indian-origin chefs and restaurants have earned multiple nominations at the 2026 James Beard Awards. London's most celebrated Indian restaurants — Dishoom, Gymkhana, Ambassadors Clubhouse — are crossing the Atlantic. The turmeric latte market alone is projected to reach $1.6 billion by 2032. And Khanna himself appeared on the TIME100 list, recognising his influence beyond the kitchen.

For the Indian diaspora, Khanna embodies something powerful: the idea that food can be a bridge between cultures without diluting either one. His cooking is unapologetically Indian in flavour while cosmopolitan in technique and presentation. His philanthropy — including massive food-distribution drives during COVID-19 that fed millions across India — demonstrates that culinary fame can be leveraged for tangible social impact.

## What It Means for NRIs

"No words to express my feelings today — from the bylanes of Amritsar to the stage at Harvard University," Khanna said. "Thank you, Boston, for so much love. Heading back to New York with a full heart."

For the millions of NRIs who grew up watching their parents' cuisine dismissed as "too spicy" or relegated to the ethnic aisle, Khanna's trajectory from Amritsar to Harvard Yard is more than a personal success story. It is evidence that the food of the subcontinent — with its complexity, its regional depth, its millennia of accumulated technique — is finally being met with the respect it has always deserved. The Harvard award is not just for Vikas Khanna. It is for every desi parent who packed methi thepla for a road trip and every NRI kid who once hid their dabba at school. Indian food is no longer asking for a seat at the table. It is setting the table.
